stem: Descartes’ first secure foothold in Meditation II is the claim that he has a body.
fix: The first foothold is the cogito — that he exists (as a thinking thing). Knowledge of body comes much later, in Meditation VI.

stem: Substance dualism is the view that minds are non-physical things, and that mental properties are properties of those non-physical things.
According to physicalism as characterized in class, two worlds that are exactly alike physically must also be exactly alike mentally.
The divisibility argument depends on the claim that bodies are divisible while the mind is not.
The method of doubt in Meditation I is meant to show that we know nothing at all.
fix: It’s a method for finding beliefs that survive even the most extreme doubt (the supreme deceiver), so that a secure system can be rebuilt from them.

stem: The mind/brain identity theory says that mental properties are properties of physical objects — specifically, brains.
Which of the following best states the conclusion of Descartes’ conceivability argument in Meditation VI (the one on p. 29)?
options: The mind cannot think without the body’s help.
The mind and the body are distinct things, each of which could exist without the other.
The mind and the body are one and the same substance, considered two ways.
Bodies cannot be doubted, but minds can.

stem: Descartes argues: I can clearly and distinctly conceive of myself existing without a body; so I could exist without a body; so I am not my body. Which premise do Smart and later critics attack?
options: That the body is divisible.
That whatever I can clearly and distinctly conceive is possible.
That God is not a deceiver about mathematics.
That animals lack minds.

stem: What does the cogito establish, according to Descartes?
options: That he can’t falsely believe that he exists.
That he has a body, since he can feel it.
That other people exist.
That the physical world is roughly as it appears.

stem: Which of the following is a way of characterizing dualism about the mental?
options: A full physical description of the world would not be a full description of the world.
Minds are identical to brains, but brains are special.
There is nothing to the world over and above the physical.
Mental vocabulary can be translated into physical vocabulary.

stem: A substance dualist and a property dualist disagree about which of the following?
options: Whether mental properties are properties of physical objects (like brains).
Whether there are any non-physical properties.
Whether pain is correlated with brain activity.
Whether physics is a successful science.

stem: In Meditation II, after the cogito, what does Descartes conclude he can be certain he is?
options: A body that happens to think.
A thinking thing.
A soul united to a body.
An immortal substance.

stem: Descartes’ first unshakeable foothold in Meditation II — “I think, therefore I am” — is known as the ______.
Descartes concludes in Meditation II that he is, essentially, a ______ thing.
Physicalism is the view that there is nothing to the world ______.
Descartes’ general methodological device in Meditation I: imagine a supremely powerful ______ trying to lead me astray, and ask what I can still be certain of.
Elisabeth’s challenge to Descartes was that an immaterial soul could not have thoughts.
fix: Her challenge was about causation: how can a soul that is only a thinking (unextended) substance bring about voluntary bodily motion?

stem: The first premise of Elisabeth’s argument — that how a thing moves depends only on how much it is pushed, how it is pushed, and the shape/surface of what pushes it — reflects the physics of 1643 and is not something today’s physicists would accept.
Epiphenomenalism holds that mental events cause physical events but physical events never cause mental events.
fix: It’s the reverse: body → mind only. Mental events are caused but are themselves causally idle.

stem: Parallelism (Leibniz) denies that there is any causal interaction between the mental and the physical in either direction.
Descartes’ reply to Elisabeth was to give a detailed mechanical account of how the soul pushes on the body.
fix: He treats the union of soul and body, and the causal relation it allows, as primitive — not explained in terms of, or in need of explanation by, anything else.

stem: The argument from causal closure needs the premise that every physical event already has a sufficient physical cause.

One version of the challenge Elisabeth’s letters raise for Cartesian dualism: the dualist owes an account of why a given soul’s mental events cause motions in one particular body rather than another — and there is no story to tell in terms of what happens in the space between them, as there is for ordinary physical causes.
In Elisabeth’s argument, why can’t a non-physical substance cause a physical object to move?
options: Because causing motion requires contact and shape, and non-physical substances have no location and no extension.
Because non-physical substances don’t exist.
Because souls, lacking extension, could cause motion only by thought, which is too weak to move matter.
Because the soul and the body can never be in the same place at the same time.

stem: The ‘two guns’ example is used to illustrate which problem for dualism?
options: That the dualist can’t say why this soul’s mental events affect this body rather than some other one — there is no spatiotemporal chain linking them, as there is for each gun and its victim.
That mental causes would make physical effects overdetermined.
That other minds can’t be known from behavior.
That souls can’t be divided.

stem: The causal exclusion argument against dualism says that, if dualism is true, mental-to-physical causation would have to be:
options: An implausible kind of systematic overdetermination — effects with two distinct sufficient causes — or else redundant.
Impossible, because souls have no location.
Explained by pre-established harmony.
A violation of the conservation of energy.

stem: Which of the dualist’s options for how the mental and the physical interact denies that the hurt-y character of experiences of pain causes the yell?
options: Interactionism
Epiphenomenalism
Substance dualism in general
Physicalism

stem: Which premise of the causal exclusion argument against dualism does epiphenomenalism reject?
options: The causal closure of the physical.
That mental events aren’t identical to physical events.
That there is a lot of mental-to-physical causation.
That there isn’t much systematic overdetermination.

stem: Princess ______ pressed Descartes, in letters of 1643, on how a merely thinking substance could bring about voluntary bodily motion.
Epiphenomenalism says that physical events cause mental events, but mental events ______.
An effect is overdetermined when it has ______.
accept: two causes each of which is sufficient

stem: Leibniz’s parallelism (aka ‘pre-established harmony’) says that the mental and the physical ______.
answer: don’t causally interact at all; they run in a harmony arranged by God
accept: don’t causally interact at all; they run in a harmony arranged by God

stem: Descartes’ reply to Elisabeth was to treat the union of soul and body as primitive — that is, as something ______.
answer: not to be explained in terms of anything else
accept: not explained in terms of anything
not to be explained in terms of anything else

stem: Ryle’s “Official Doctrine” is his name for behaviorism.
fix: It’s his name for the Cartesian picture — substance dualism, “the dogma of the Ghost in the Machine.”

stem: A category mistake, in Ryle’s sense, is treating something as belonging to a logical type it doesn’t belong to — e.g. asking where the University is after being shown all the colleges and libraries.
On Ryle’s picture, mental states are single-track dispositions of the form ‘produce response R in circumstance C’.
fix: They’re multi-track dispositions: many different behaviors in many different circumstances (Jane Austen on the heroine of Pride and Prejudice; hardness as a physical precedent).

stem: You could be a methodological behaviorist without being an analytical behaviorist.
Putnam’s super-spartan is a person who is in pain and displays no pain behavior.
Although Ryle mentions Elisabeth’s interaction worry, the objection he leans hardest on is epistemic: on the Official Doctrine, our beliefs about other people’s minds are on bad epistemic footing.
‘How do you know the Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776?’ is a metaphysical question.
fix: It’s epistemological. The metaphysical question is what makes it the case that it was adopted then (the proceedings, votes, etc.).

stem: Why does Ryle single out the Average Taxpayer example as the one he really wants for the parallel with the mind?
options: Because it’s a mistake that someone who’s basically competent with the concept could make.
Because, like the mind, the Average Taxpayer is unobservable, so the parallel with private mental states is closest.
Because it is the only example in which the mistaken entity is a person, as a mind is.
Because it is the example that shows a category mistake can be harmless.

stem: On Ryle’s speculation, why did Descartes make the category mistake?
options: Torn between endorsing mechanics and refusing to see humans as clockwork, he described minds in an ‘obverse vocabulary’: bits of not-clockwork.
He mistook the mind’s privacy for a difference in substance, inferring from ‘I can’t observe your thoughts’ to ‘thoughts are non-physical things’.
He generalized from the cogito: since he could doubt his body but not his mind, he concluded the mind was a second mechanism obeying its own laws.
He lacked the concept of a disposition, and so took every mental word to name an inner episode.

stem: Analytical behaviorism is the view that:
options: Psychology should only run experiments on behavior.
The meanings of mental terms are to be given in behavioral terms.
Mental states cause behavior.
Behavior is caused by brain states.

stem: Which of the following is Ryle’s own reason for saying the caricature ‘pain = a disposition to jump around and scream’ is wrong?
options: Mental dispositions are multi-track: many different responses in many different situations.
Pain is an occurrence, not a disposition, so it can’t be analyzed dispositionally at all.
The disposition to scream is suppressible, as the super-spartan shows.
Pain-talk is really about brain processes, so behavior is beside the point.

stem: On the Official Doctrine as Ryle describes it, mental things are:
options: Located in space and publicly observable.
Not located in space, not subject to physical laws, and observable only by their owner.
Identical to brain processes.
Dispositions to behave.

stem: Ryle’s deliberately abusive name for the Cartesian picture: the dogma of the ______ in the Machine.
A category mistake, in Ryle’s sense, is treating something as ______.
answer: belonging to a logical type (category) it doesn’t belong to — e.g. as a further thing of the same kind as the things it is related to
accept: another thing of the same kind
a further thing of the same kind
a logical type it does not belong to
belonging to a logical type it doesn’t belong to
belonging to a logical type (category) it doesn’t belong to — e.g. as a further thing of the same kind as the things it is related to

stem: Hilary Putnam’s imagined people who feel pain but never show it are the super-______.
Epistemology is the study of ______; metaphysics is the study of ______.
accept: how we know; what there is
knowledge; the fundamental structure of reality

stem: Ryle’s example of a category mistake made by someone who sees the colleges, libraries and playing fields and then asks to see the ______.
Smart’s identity theory claims that “after-image” means “brain process of sort X.”
fix: It’s explicitly not a thesis about meaning (or translation, or logic/grammar). The identity is like lightning = electrical discharge: true, but not a matter of what the words mean.

stem: The type–type identity theory entails the token–token identity theory, but not vice versa.
Leibniz’s Law (the indiscernibility of identicals) says that if x and y share all their properties, then x = y.
fix: That’s the identity of indiscernibles — the converse, and much more controversial. Leibniz’s Law says: if x = y, then every property of x is a property of y.

stem: “Ronald Reagan is an actor; President Reagan is a politician; so they are different men” is a valid application of Leibniz’s Law.
fix: Being a politician doesn’t rule out being an actor. A Leibniz’s Law argument needs a property one thing has and the other lacks, not just two different properties.

stem: Objection: an illiterate peasant can talk perfectly well about his after-images while knowing nothing about brain processes — so after-images can’t be brain processes. Smart’s reply is that a person can know something is an A without knowing it is a B, as with the Morning Star and the Evening Star.
Being able to immediately and uncontroversially imagine that water isn’t H₂O shows that water could, metaphysically, have failed to be H₂O.
fix: Discovered identities are exactly cases where the negation is conceivable (epistemically possible) but, if the identity is true, not metaphysically possible.

stem: Leibniz’s Law implies that nothing can change its properties over time.
fix: The properties have to be compared at the same time. The unscratched laptop last year and the scratched laptop now are one laptop.

stem: “We bought identical laptops” uses ‘identical’ in the same sense Smart uses it when he says “sensations are identical to brain processes.”
fix: That’s qualitative identity (exact similarity, two laptops). Smart means numerical identity — one and the same thing.

stem: “It’s possible I was born on the moon,” said by someone who doesn’t remember where they were born and has lost their birth records, uses ‘possible’ in the epistemic sense.
Why does Smart say the identity theory isn’t *really* one more way of explaining the correlation between sensations and brain processes?
options: Because correlations require two things, and identity says there is only one.
Because the identity theory explains the correlation as a common-cause structure.
Because a correlation between a sensation and a brain process would require a non-physical law, which Smart rejects.
Because correlations hold between types, and Smart’s thesis is only about tokens.

stem: “Aunt Lobelia is in my mind (I’m thinking of her). Aunt Lobelia is not in my brain (go look). So my mind isn’t my brain.” What goes wrong with this attempted application of Leibniz’s Law?
options: Equivocation: no single reading of ‘in’ makes both premises true.
The two properties aren’t incompatible: ‘x is F, y is G’ doesn’t show that y lacks F.
The ‘property’ concerns how someone represents the thing (like ‘is believed by Lex to be a threat’), and Leibniz’s Law arguments break down for such properties.
The properties are being compared at different times.

stem: “Lex Luthor believes Superman is a threat; Lex Luthor doesn’t believe Clark Kent is a threat; so Superman ≠ Clark Kent.” What goes wrong with this attempted application of Leibniz’s Law?
options: The ‘property’ concerns how Lex represents the thing — and Leibniz’s Law arguments break down for properties like being believed to be a threat, being known about, being feared.
The two properties aren’t incompatible: being believed to be a threat doesn’t rule out not being believed to be a threat.
‘Threat’ means something different in the two premises.
The properties are being compared at different times: Lex’s beliefs changed between the premises.

stem: Smart considers this objection: ‘A molecular movement can be swift or circular; an experience can’t be; so experiences aren’t molecular movements.’ His diagnosis is:
options: It isn’t obvious that an experience can be circular, but that isn’t the same as its being obvious that it can’t — the properties haven’t been shown to be incompatible.
‘Swift’ means one thing of movements and another of experiences, so the premises equivocate.
‘Swift’ and ‘circular’ describe how the movement is represented, so Leibniz’s Law doesn’t apply.
The objector has misidentified the property-bearer: it’s the after-image, not the experience, that is circular.

stem: Pryor’s amnesiac professor imagines a world with himself in it and Jim Pryor gone. The example is used to show that:
options: One can conceive something that is necessarily false, so conceivability doesn’t guarantee (metaphysical) possibility.
Personal identity over time is a matter of memory, since losing his memory makes him a different person.
One can doubt one’s own existence, contrary to the cogito.
Names like ‘Jim Pryor’ have no meaning for someone who doesn’t know who they refer to.

stem: Which of these is Smart’s stated motivation for the identity theory?
options: Parsimony: if sensations were non-physical, they’d be nomological danglers attached by laws unlike anything known to science.
Introspection reveals nothing non-physical, so there is nothing for a dualist to point to.
The conceivability of sensations without brain processes shows they must be identical.
The discovery that pain is correlated with C-fiber firing proves the identity directly.

stem: How many words are on this line: pain pain pain? Which answer correctly applies the type/token distinction?
options: Three word-tokens (three inscriptions) of one word-type.
Three word-types of one word-token.
Three tokens and three types, since each inscription is its own word.
One token and one type, since it is the same word repeated.

stem: Suppose that the android Commander Data and I both feel pain, but my pains are all instances of a carbon-based neurological type and Data’s are instances of a silicon-based (or positronic) type. Which version of the identity theory can still be true?
options: Type–type only.
Token–token only.
Both.
Neither.

stem: One of Smart’s imagined objectors says: ‘I can imagine myself turned to stone and yet still having aches and pains; so sensations aren’t brain processes.’ Descartes’ Meditation VI argument and this objection share which premise?
options: That minds are divisible.
That whatever I can conceive is possible.
That brain processes are public.
That sensations are private.

stem: Which of these is a posteriori?
options: Triangles have three sides
Wild platypuses are found only in Australia
If x = y then every property of x is a property of y

stem: Why does Smart think we should avoid positing ‘nomological danglers’? Because ______.
answer: they would have to be hooked onto the physical world by ultimate laws unlike anything in science — an unparsimonious, suspicious addition
accept: laws of a very strange sort

stem: Leibniz’s Law (the indiscernibility of identicals) says: if x = y, then ______.
answer: every property x has, y has too
accept: every property x has, y has too
whatever is true of x is true of y
x and y have all the same properties
every property of x is a property of y
x and y have exactly the same properties
any property of one is a property of the other

stem: Something is knowable a priori if it can be known ______; something is a posteriori if it can be known only ______.
accept: from the armchair; by going and looking

stem: ‘It’s possible that P’ in the epistemic sense means (approximately) ______; in the metaphysical sense it means (approximately) ______.
answer: for all I know, P; the world could have been such that P

for all we know; could have been otherwise

stem: In the kind of machine table that features in machine-table functionalism, each state is specified entirely by its relations to inputs, outputs, and other states — nothing about what the machine is made of.
Functionalism, all by itself, is committed to physicalism.
fix: It isn’t: a functional role could in principle be occupied by non-physical stuff. (Most functionalists are physicalists, but that’s an extra commitment.)

stem: One of the main objections to functionalism is its inability to allow for the multiple realizability of mental states.
fix: Allowing for multiple realizability is one of functionalism’s main selling points; it’s the type–type identity theory that has trouble with it.

stem: Ramsification is a technique for defining a whole set of terms at once, by their relations to each other and to things outside the theory.
In Ramsified functionalism, we first pick one mental state to give a functional definition of, and then define the other states in terms of that first one.
fix: All the states are defined at once, by their relations to each other and to inputs and outputs; no state is defined first.

stem: The functional roles that feature in functionalist theories of mind are only forward-looking: the functional roles associated with mental states concern what a state causes, not what causes it.
fix: A functional role includes both what typically causes the state and what the state typically causes (behavior and other mental states).

stem: Functionalism is designed to allow for stoics and pretenders: being in pain without displaying pain behavior, and displaying pain behavior without being in pain.
Which of the following is NOT an advantage functionalists claim for their view over behaviorism and the identity theory?
options: It guarantees that there is something it is like to be in each mental state.
It allows the same mental state to show up in creatures made of very different stuff.
It lets mental states be characterized partly by their connections to other mental states.
It allows mental states to be internal states that can be present without their characteristic behavior.

stem: In Fodor’s functionalist characterization of a Coke machine in terms of two possible states, S1 and S2, why isn’t the interdefinition of S1 and S2 a vicious circle?
options: Because the whole table — the two states together with their inputs and outputs — fixes both states at once; the connections to inputs and outputs anchor the interdefinition.
Because S1 and S2 are ultimately defined in terms of what the machine is made of.
Because only S2 is defined in terms of S1; S1 is defined independently, by its outputs alone.
Because each state is defined by its behavior alone, with no reference to the other state.

stem: Which problem for behaviorism does functionalism fix by letting mental states be characterized partly in terms of other mental states?
options: The ‘what’s the characteristic behavior for believing it’s raining?’ problem — there’s no distinctive behavior for a single state, because behavior depends on what else you believe and want.
The super-spartan: a mental state present with no manifest behavior at all.
The interaction problem: how a non-physical mind could cause physical behavior.
The problem of other minds: our only evidence for others’ mental states is their behavior.

stem: An ‘identity theory’ for vending machines — the analogue of the mind/brain identity theory — would:
options: Put two machines that run the same machine table using different physical mechanisms into different states.
Say the machine has no states.
Be the same as functionalism about vending machines.
Deny that the machines dispense anything.

stem: Machine-table functionalism characterizes a mind by a table whose states are total states — the system’s entire mental condition at a moment. Which of the following is hard for such a table to capture?
options: A generalization like: believing it’s raining plus wanting to stay dry tends to cause umbrella-fetching, whatever else is going on in the mind.
That the system is in exactly one state at any moment.
That the same table can be realized in very different stuff.
That each state is defined by its relations to inputs, outputs, and the other states.

stem: Stalnaker: “To believe that P is to be disposed to act in ways that would tend to satisfy one’s desires, whatever they are, in a world in which P … were true.” This characterizes belief in terms of:
options: Its typical effects — what it leads the believer to do, together with their desires.
Its typical causes — what typically brings the belief about.
Brain states.
Behavior alone, with no mention of other mental states.

stem: A machine table specifies, for each state and each input, ______.
answer: what output the machine produces and what state it goes into next

the response and the new state
the output and the resulting state

what it does and which state it goes to
what the machine outputs and its next state
what output the machine produces and what state it goes into next

stem: To say that pain is multiply realizable is to say that ______.
answer: the same mental state can be realized in very different kinds of physical stuff

does not require any particular physical
can be implemented in different physical systems
can be realized in different kinds of physical stuff
can be had by creatures with different physical make-ups
the same mental state can be realized in very different kinds of physical stuff

stem: According to functionalism, mental states are individuated in terms of their network of causal connections to ______.
answer: stimuli (inputs), behavior (outputs), and other mental states
accept: inputs, outputs, and other mental states
stimuli, behavior, and other mental states

its causes, its effects, and other mental states

stem: In Frank Jackson’s thought experiment in “Epiphenomenal Qualia”, Mary knows every physical fact about color vision before she leaves the black-and-white room.
‘Conscious’ in the what-it’s-like sense means the same as ‘awake’.
fix: Dreams are conscious in the what-it’s-like sense but not in the ‘awake’ sense.

stem: Spectrum inversion is the possibility of two people who are functionally alike but whose color experiences differ in qualitative character.
Jackson’s conclusion in the knowledge argument is that there are some non-physical facts.
On Jackson’s telling, what Mary learns when she sees the tomato is only a fact about herself.
fix: She also learns something about other people — what their experiences of red have been like all along — though she already knew everything about their brains.

stem: Nagel’s bat example is meant to show that there is nothing it is like to be a bat.
fix: The opposite: there is (almost certainly) something it’s like to be a bat, probably very different from what it’s like to be us, and that character isn’t fixed by fixing the functional facts.

stem: The ‘absent qualia’ worry is that there could be a creature functionally just like us in which ‘the lights are off’ — no qualitative experience at all.
Which premise would a physicalist most naturally attack in the knowledge argument (1. Mary knows every physical fact; 2. Mary doesn’t know every fact; 3. So there are non-physical facts)?
options: Premise 2 — deny that what Mary gains on leaving the room is knowledge of a new fact (rather than, say, a new ability or a new way of grasping an old fact).
Premise 1 — deny that completed physics counts as ‘every physical fact’, since it leaves out facts about functional organization.
The inference — grant that she learns a non-physical fact but deny that this shows physicalism is false.
None of them; the physicalist should accept the argument and become an epiphenomenalist.

stem: Why does the knowledge argument make trouble for functionalism and not just the identity theory?
options: Because every fact about functional organization — what each state is caused by, causes, and does — is something Mary would have already learned in the course of learning all the physical facts.
Because functionalism is a form of dualism about qualia.
Because functional roles are discovered a posteriori, and Mary in the room only knows a priori facts.
Because Mary’s new knowledge is of a functional role she couldn’t occupy in the room.

stem: Qualia are:
options: Brain processes in the visual cortex.
Dispositions to behave.
The what-it’s-like properties of experiences — how they feel ‘from the inside’.
Beliefs about colors.

stem: The absent-qualia argument against functionalism (‘I can imagine a system with all the right functional states but with no qualia’) rests its weight in the same place as Descartes’ Meditation VI argument and Smart’s imagined objector who says, ‘I can imagine myself turned to stone yet still having pains.’ Where?
options: On the step from conceivability to (metaphysical) possibility.
On Leibniz’s Law: the imagined system has a property (lacking experience) that we lack.
On multiple realizability: functional states can be realized without brains.
On the a priori/a posteriori distinction: functional facts are knowable a priori.

stem: Which of these is the inverted-qualia objection to functionalism?
options: Functionally identical creatures could have no experience at all.
Functionally identical creatures could have experiences with different qualitative character — your experience of red is like my experience of green.
Mary learns a new fact.
Bats can’t be functionally characterized.

stem: What problem for functionalism is Nagel’s bat supposed to raise?
options: The qualitative character of bat experience doesn’t seem to be fixed by fixing all the functional facts.
We cannot know whether bats are conscious, so functionalism is unfalsifiable.
Bat echolocation has no functional characterization, so functionalism is incomplete.
Since there is nothing it is like to be a bat, qualia aren’t essential to mentality.

stem: Qualia are the ______ properties of experiences.
Thomas Nagel’s famous paper asks what it is like to be a ______.
The spectrum-inversion scenario: two people who are functionally alike but whose ______.
answer: color experiences differ in qualitative character — one’s red is like the other’s green
accept: red is like the other’s green
color experiences differ in qualitative character — one’s red is like the other’s green

stem: An absent-qualia case is one in which a system functionally just like us ______.
answer: has no qualitative experience at all — ‘the lights are off’
accept: there is nothing it is like
has no qualitative experience at all — ‘the lights are off’

stem: Analytic functionalism gets its functional definitions of mental terms from the common-sense platitudes of folk psychology.
Psychofunctionalism takes the functional roles that define mental states from our best empirical cognitive psychology, not just from common knowledge.
Eliminativism says that beliefs and desires exist and are identical to brain states.
fix: That’s the identity theory’s hope (reduction). Eliminativism says folk psychology is a false theory to be replaced, as chemistry replaced alchemy; beliefs and desires may not exist.

stem: ‘Blanca wants coffee’ (an example from the Stanford Encyclopedia reading on functionalism) = she is disposed to order coffee when offered, if she has no stronger desire to avoid coffee. What makes this an analytic functionalist analysis rather than a behaviorist one?
options: It mentions another mental state (a competing desire), and the extra condition is itself a platitude.
It is phrased in terms of a disposition rather than actual behavior.
It specifies the stimulus (being offered coffee) rather than only the response.
It is drawn from empirical psychology rather than common sense.

stem: Block’s economy of Bolivia example (from the Stanford Encyclopedia reading on functionalism) is an objection to:
options: Analytic functionalism, for being too liberal — a short list of platitudes might be satisfied by something with no mind.
Psychofunctionalism, for being too chauvinistic — it excludes systems built differently from us.
Eliminativism, for being self-refuting — it must believe its own thesis.
The identity theory, for identifying economic states with physical states.

stem: Which of the following is the distinctive claim of eliminativism?
options: Folk psychology is a radically false theory; completed neuroscience will replace it rather than reduce it, and beliefs and desires may turn out not to exist.
Folk psychology is roughly true, and its states will be identified with brain states by a completed neuroscience.
Mental terms are defined by platitudes, but the platitudes may be refined by science.
Mental states are defined by their roles in our best empirical psychology, which may diverge from common sense.

stem: Folk theories meet empirical findings in different ways. Which of these is a case where science refines a folk category rather than confirming it or overturning it?
options: Science splits ‘sadness’ into sadness and clinical depression.
Bodily injury tends to cause pain.
Moving things don’t stop on their own.
Whales are fish.

stem: Analytic functionalism takes the roles that define mental states from ______.
Psychofunctionalism takes the roles that define mental states from ______.
Eliminativism says that folk psychology is ______, and that beliefs and desires ______.
answer: a false theory; may not exist at all
accept: a bad theory; may not exist
a false theory; may not exist
a false theory; may not exist at all
a radically false theory; don't exist

stem: Behaviorism, the identity theory, and functionalism are all, by definition, forms of physicalism.
fix: Functionalism isn’t committed to physicalism by itself: a role could be occupied by non-physical stuff.

stem: Which objection drives the move from the (type–type) identity theory to functionalism?
options: Multiple realizability: pain can’t be C-fiber firing if dogs, Martians, or silicon systems could be in pain.
The super-spartans: a mental state can be present without its characteristic behavior.
The pairing problem: nothing links a particular mental state to a particular body.
The knowledge argument: Mary learns something not fixed by the physical facts.

stem: Which of the following views allows mental states to be internal states that can come apart from behavior AND refuses to tie each mental state to one specific kind of physical stuff?
options: Analytical behaviorism
Type–type identity theory
Functionalism
Methodological behaviorism

stem: Which of these is an epistemological rather than a metaphysical objection to dualism?
options: Ryle’s: on the dualist picture, our beliefs about other minds rest on inference from behavior, with no direct access.
Elisabeth’s: an unextended soul can’t push an extended body.
Kim’s: nothing links this soul to this body rather than another.
The argument from causal closure: physical effects already have sufficient physical causes.

stem: ‘I know what my pain feels like without knowing anything about neurons; so my pain isn’t a neural process.’ This argument most resembles:
options: Smart’s reply to the illiterate peasant: knowing about one side of an identity without knowing about the other is no objection (the Morning Star and the Evening Star).
Elisabeth’s interaction argument: minds lack the properties needed to act on bodies.
Descartes’ Meditation VI argument: I can conceive the one without the other.
Block’s Bolivian economy: a system satisfies the role without having the state.

stem: Kind’s egg-drop example is meant to show that what makes something an egg protector is its physical material, not what it does.
fix: The reverse: successful egg protectors (bubble-wrapped tissue box, duct-taped balloons, popcorn and flour) share no physical materials; what they share is how they function.

stem: In Kind’s example, Mort the super-stoic is a potential counterexample to behaviorism: he is in pain while lacking even the disposition to engage in pain behavior.
Kind says that, strictly speaking, functionalism is compatible with dualism, since a non-physical state (a ghost’s, say) could in principle play the functional role of a mental state.
The anti-nesting principle (from the Kind reading on functionalism) says that a conscious organism cannot have parts that are themselves individually conscious of the same state.

Kind contrasts two old sayings. ‘All that glitters is not gold’: to be gold is to have a particular physical constitution (atomic number 79). ‘Build a better mousetrap’: to be a mousetrap is to do a certain job, whatever you are made of. According to Kind, functionalism says mental states are like gold — what matters is their physical constitution.
fix: Mental states are to be understood on the model of mousetraps, not gold: what matters is function, not constitution.

stem: Kind says the functionalist analysis of a mental state has three components, and that one of them is what differentiates the functionalist from the behaviorist. Which one is it that differentiates functionalism from behaviorism?
options: Relations to other mental states.
Inputs (e.g. stepping on a tack).
Outputs (e.g. grimacing, crying out).
Physical constitution.

stem: Why does Kind say it is natural to see functionalism as a version of token physicalism rather than type physicalism?
options: Because states of very different physical types can all be instances of one functional type, while each of them may still be a physical state of some type or other.
Because functionalists hold that each functional type is identical to one physical type.
Because functionalism denies that mental states are physical at all.
Because token physicalism is the only view compatible with behaviorism.

stem: In the Kind reading on functionalism, why does Block move from the homunculi-headed robot to the version with a billion people (the populations of North and South America) operating remotes?
options: Because the homunculi scenario, though coherent, couldn’t be pulled off given our physical laws, and the billion-people version makes the intuition that the system lacks qualia clearer.
Because a billion people can implement the table faster than homunculi.
Because homunculi are conscious, which would violate the anti-nesting principle.
Because the robot needs more than one bulletin board.

stem: Kind compares one functionalist reply to the absent-qualia argument with a reply to the Mary case. What is the shared move?
options: If we really imagined the system as perfectly (not approximately) implementing the table — as we must imagine Mary having all, not just lots of, physical information — the intuition would go away. Both deny that the scenario is really conceivable.
Both replies deny that conceivability entails possibility.
Both replies accept the scenario but deny that it shows anything about qualia.
Both replies invoke the anti-nesting principle.

stem: Jade and Scarlet stop at the same stop signs, sort the Uno deck the same way, and use color words alike, yet (the scenario goes) Jade has greenish experiences where Scarlet has reddish ones when they look at stop signs. What would the functionalist most want to find, according to Kind, to resist the scenario?
options: Some way the inversion would have to show up in behavior — e.g. one of them classing red as a ‘warm’ shade and the other as ‘cool’.
Proof that Jade and Scarlet have different neurons.
Evidence that synesthesia is impossible.
A demonstration that color experiences have no qualitative character.

stem: Ned Block’s example (from the Kind reading on functionalism) of a system functionally equivalent to you but intuitively lacking qualia: the ______-headed robot.
Kind’s Mort (the super-stoic) and Putnam’s super-spartan make the same point against behaviorism: a mental state can be present without any disposition to its characteristic behavior.

Both the identity theory and functionalism say that mental states are internal states — states that can be present even when the characteristic behavior isn’t. The two theories disagree about whether what makes an internal state a pain, rather than some other state, is what that state is made of.

The exclusion argument (from causal closure) and Smart’s parsimony argument both put pressure on the same thing: non-physical mental events that would need to do causal work the physical already does.
Of the views in the unit, only substance dualism holds that there are non-physical things that have mental properties.
A creature behaves exactly as a person in pain does, has internal states that play the pain role, but is made of silicon and has no C-fibers. Which theory says it is NOT in pain?
options: Type–type identity theory
Functionalism
Analytical behaviorism
Token–token identity theory

stem: Smart responds to the objection that an illiterate peasant can talk about his after-images without knowing any neuroscience. Which of these has the same logical shape, and (Smart would say) fails for the same reason?
options: ‘I know what my pain feels like without knowing any neuroscience; so my pain isn’t a neural process.’
‘A soul has no location, so it can’t push a body.’
‘Pain can be realized without C-fibers, so pain isn’t C-fiber firing.’
‘A system functionally like me could lack experience, so experience isn’t functional role.’

stem: Which view would be most embarrassed by the discovery that an octopus, with a radically different nervous system, feels pain?
options: Type–type identity theory
Functionalism
Substance dualism
Token–token identity theory

stem: The objection to behaviorism from Mort (the super-stoic in the Kind reading) or the super-spartan, and the objection to the identity theory from multiple realizability, both motivate the same successor theory: ______.
Something is necessary if it ______.
answer: couldn’t have failed to be true
accept: couldn’t have failed to be true
could not have failed to be true
is true in every possible world

stem: Something is contingent if it ______.
accept: could have failed to be true
is true but didn’t have to be

stem: Reading ‘is’ as strict (numerical) identity — one and the same thing — which of the following is true?
options: The Morning Star is the Evening Star.
My car is your car — same make, model, year, and color.
The dime in my pocket is the dime in yours; you couldn’t tell them apart.
Today’s lecture is yesterday’s lecture, repeated word for word.

stem: Which of the following is true if ‘is’ is read as qualitative identity (exact similarity), but false if ‘is’ is read as strict (numerical) identity?
options: My laptop is your laptop — we bought the same model.
Lightning is an electrical discharge.
Clark Kent is Superman.
7 is the smallest prime greater than 5.

stem: Give an example of an a priori truth (one that doesn’t appear elsewhere on this exam): ______.
answer: e.g. 2 + 2 = 4; all bachelors are unmarried; nothing is both round and square

stem: Give an example of an a posteriori truth (one that doesn’t appear elsewhere on this exam): ______.
answer: e.g. Paris is the capital of France; water boils at 100°C at sea level; it rained yesterday

stem: Give an example of a necessary truth (one that doesn’t appear elsewhere on this exam): ______.
answer: e.g. 2 + 2 = 4; all bachelors are unmarried; everything is identical to itself

stem: Give an example of a contingent truth (one that doesn’t appear elsewhere on this exam): ______.
answer: e.g. I am in New Jersey right now; it is raining; Rutgers has a philosophy department
